title: Grade 1 Maths: What Your Child Should Know by Year End + Free Quiz
meta_title: Grade 1 Maths Syllabus: What Your Child Should Know
meta_desc: A parent's guide to the whole Grade 1 maths syllabus, what mastery looks like in each strand, red flags to watch, and a free readiness quiz for your child.
excerpt: Numbers to 100, sums within 20, shapes, time to the hour, coins. Here is the full map of Grade 1 maths, what ‘mastered’ actually looks like for each part, and the one warning sign to catch early.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
A parent messaged me in June, three weeks into the new session: ‘My daughter can count to 100, so she is ahead in maths, right?’ I get some version of that question every year, and the honest answer is — counting to 100 is one strand out of about nine. What maths a Grade 1 child should know by the end of the year is a good deal wider than most parents expect, and it is easy to feel lost when the school sends home a single line of homework with no map of where it all leads. So here is the map.

This is the whole Grade 1 maths syllabus as CBSE and NCERT lay it out, strand by strand. For each one I have written what ‘mastered’ genuinely looks like by March, and the single red flag that tells you to slow down and reteach. I am deliberately not going deep on any one strand here — each has its own guide — because the point of this page is to help you see the year as a whole.

The nine strands of Grade 1 maths

Think of the year as building in this rough order. Numbers come first because almost everything else leans on them.

1. Numbers and counting to 100

By year end a child should count forward and backward to 100, count in tens (10, 20, 30…), and read and write any two-digit number. The quiet skill that matters most is counting on from any number — starting at 47 and going 48, 49, 50 — not always restarting from one.

Red flag: a child who can chant ‘one to hundred’ like a song but cannot tell you what comes after 68 when asked cold. That is memorised sound, not number sense.

2. Place value (tens and ones)

They should see 34 as 3 tens and 4 ones, not just ‘three-four’. Bundling ten straws into a bunch and understanding that the bunch is worth ten is the whole idea.

Red flag: writing 52 as 502 — a sign they are hearing ‘fifty’ and ‘two’ as separate numbers rather than a structured one.

3. Addition and subtraction within 20

This is the heavy lifting of the year. Mastery means adding and subtracting within 20 using strategies — number bonds to ten, making ten, doubles — rather than counting every finger. Word problems like ‘Riya had 8 sweets and ate 3’ should feel routine.

Red flag: still counting all on fingers for 8 + 5 in the final term. Fingers are fine in June; they should be fading by February.

4. 2D and 3D shapes

Name circle, triangle, square and rectangle, and recognise a ball (sphere), box (cuboid) and can (cylinder) as their solid cousins. Sorting objects by shape counts here too.

Red flag: calling every four-sided shape a square. Squares and rectangles get mixed up constantly — worth gently separating.

5. Patterns

Continue and create simple patterns — red-blue-red-blue, or triangle-circle-triangle. Patterns look like play but they are early algebra, teaching a child to spot and extend a rule.

Red flag: can copy a pattern you make but cannot predict what comes next. Prediction is the actual skill.

6. Measurement: length, weight and capacity

At this age it is all non-standard and comparative — longer or shorter, heavier or lighter, holds more or less. Measuring a table in handspans is exactly right for Grade 1; centimetres come later.

Red flag: confusing ‘big’ with ‘heavy’. A large empty box feels light, and noticing that is real learning.

7. Time to the hour

Read a clock at o’clock — 3 o’clock, 7 o’clock — and order daily events (breakfast, school, dinner). Days of the week in order belong here too.

Red flag: reading the minute hand instead of the hour hand at o’clock.

8. Money

Recognise Indian coins and notes up to ₹10 and know that a ₹5 coin is worth more than two ₹1 coins. Simple shop-play — ‘this pencil costs ₹3, here is ₹5’ — does the teaching for you.

Red flag: judging value by coin size, thinking a big ₹1 coin beats a small ₹5 one.

9. Simple data handling

Sort a set of objects and answer ‘which group has more?’ from a simple picture chart. This is the earliest seed of graphs.

Red flag: counting the tallest column as ‘more’ without actually counting the items.

What mastery looks like, strand by strand

If you want one glance-able summary to stick on the fridge, here it is.

StrandWhat mastery looks like by year end
Numbers to 100Counts forward, backward and in tens; reads and writes any two-digit number
Place valueExplains 34 as 3 tens and 4 ones using bundles
Add & subtract to 20Uses bonds and making-ten, not finger-counting; solves simple word problems
2D & 3D shapesNames basic flat shapes and matches them to solids
PatternsContinues and creates a pattern, and predicts what comes next
MeasurementCompares length, weight and capacity in everyday, non-standard units
TimeReads o’clock times and orders daily events and weekdays
MoneyIdentifies coins to ₹10 and compares their value, not their size
DataSorts objects and reads ‘more or less’ from a picture chart

How to cover every strand without the overwhelm

Here is the counter-intuitive part: you do not need nine separate activities. A single trip to the vegetable market covers counting, money, weight and ‘which pile has more’ in fifteen minutes. Everyday maths beats worksheets in June and July, when the ideas are new.

  • Count the stairs, the chapatis, the parked cars — count on from a number, do not always restart from one.
  • Let your child pay with coins at a shop and check the change.
  • Ask ‘which is heavier?’ before you buy, then test it by holding both.
  • Read the clock aloud at o’clock moments — dinner is at 8 o’clock.

By the second half of the year, though, written practice earns its place. Children need to see numbers on paper, choose a strategy themselves, and build the neat handwriting habits that Grade 2 assumes. quiz.title: Grade 1 Maths Readiness Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions spanning counting, shapes, addition, time and money. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: A mixed Grade 1 maths readiness check

questions.explanation: Counting on from 68 gives the next number, 69.

questions.q: How many tens and ones are in 34?
questions.explanation: The 3 stands for 3 tens (30) and the 4 stands for 4 ones, so 30 + 4 = 34.
Make ten: take 2 from the 5 to turn 8 into 10, then add the leftover 3. 10 + 3 = 13.

questions.q: Which shape is round with no corners?
questions.explanation: A circle is perfectly round and has no corners or straight sides.

questions.q: The short hand points to 7 and the long hand points to 12. What is the time?
questions.explanation: At o’clock the long hand is on 12; the short hand shows the hour, which is 7. So it is 7 o’clock.
A ₹5 coin is worth 5 rupees, more than three ₹1 coins (3 rupees). Value comes from the number, not the coin’s size.

questions.q: What comes next in the pattern: circle, square, circle, square, ___?
questions.explanation: The rule alternates circle then square, so after square comes circle again.

questions.q: Which group has more: 6 apples or 9 apples?
questions.explanation: 9 is greater than 6, so the group of 9 apples has more.

faq.q: What maths should a Grade 1 child know by the end of the year?
faq.a: Counting and writing numbers to 100, place value with tens and ones, addition and subtraction within 20, basic 2D and 3D shapes, simple patterns, comparing length, weight and capacity, telling time to the hour, recognising coins to ₹10, and sorting objects into simple picture charts.

faq.q: Is my child behind if they still count on fingers?
faq.a: In the first term, no — fingers make maths concrete and every child starts there. The concern is only if finger-counting is still the main method for sums like 8 + 5 in the final term, which signals they need more work on number bonds and making ten.

faq.q: Which Grade 1 strand should I focus on most?
faq.a: Number sense — counting on, place value and bonds to ten. These underpin addition, subtraction, money and measurement, so time spent here pays off across every other strand for years.

faq.q: Does Grade 1 maths follow the NCERT and CBSE syllabus?
faq.a: Yes. The nine strands in this guide map to the CBSE and NCERT Class 1 maths curriculum. Most state boards and private schools follow the same broad outline, so the milestones here apply widely across India.
